notes.text: For more than 8, cook the spaghetti in two pots, each with the full amount of water and salt, so the water comes back to a boil quickly, and use your biggest pot for the sauce.

callback.body: You've simmered a pot of vegetables before: small, lazy bubbles that cook things gently. Marinara uses the same simmer to turn a can of tomatoes into a thick, sweet sauce.

move.title: Build it in layers
move.body: Building a sauce means adding flavors one layer at a time, each cooked just enough before the next goes in. Today you'll soften onion in olive oil, add garlic, then tomatoes, and simmer it into marinara, a simple Italian tomato sauce. A little starchy pasta water helps it cling to every strand of spaghetti.

why.title: Slow first, fast second
why.body: Onion needs several minutes to turn soft and sweet. Garlic needs about one, and it burns soon after. That's why the onion goes in first and the garlic joins it at the end: each one gets the time it needs, and nothing scorches.

why.title: Simmering thickens and sweetens
why.body: As the sauce bubbles gently, water escapes as steam. Less water means thicker sauce and stronger flavor, and the sharp, tinny taste of canned tomatoes softens. A spoon dragged across the pan leaves a path when it's ready.

why.title: Salty water, tasty pasta
why.body: Pasta soaks up the water it cooks in. If the water is salted, the pasta is seasoned all the way through. If it isn't, no amount of sauce on top fixes plain-tasting noodles.

why.title: Pasta water is the glue
why.body: Cooking pasta releases starch into the water, turning it a little cloudy. A splash of it in the sauce helps the sauce stick to the spaghetti instead of sliding off and puddling in the bowl.

wrong.sign: The garlic turned brown and smells bitter
wrong.fix: Start over with fresh oil and garlic. Burnt garlic makes the whole sauce bitter.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and watery
wrong.fix: Keep simmering, uncovered, a few more minutes, stirring now and then.

wrong.sign: The sauce tastes sour or sharp
wrong.fix: Simmer a few minutes longer, add a pinch of salt, and taste again. A tiny pinch of sugar helps too.

wrong.sign: The spaghetti is stuck together in a clump
wrong.fix: Stir it in the first two minutes of cooking, and use a big pot of water. Toss clumped pasta with the sauce and a splash of pasta water to loosen it.

quiz.q: Why does the garlic go in after the onion, not with it?
choices: Garlic cooks fast and burns if it's in too long
quiz.explain: Onion needs minutes to soften; garlic needs about one. Adding it later keeps it from burning.

quiz.q: Why save a cup of pasta water?
choices: Its starch helps the sauce cling to the pasta
quiz.explain: Starchy pasta water helps sauce stick to every strand.

substitutions.note: Gluten-free spaghetti turns soft quickly. Start tasting it 2 minutes before the box says.

steps.text: Fill the large pot with the water, cover it, and set it over high heat to come to a boil. It takes a while, so start it first.
steps.tip: Fill the pot at the sink, then carry it to the stove before it's hot. Never carry a pot of boiling water.

steps.text: Cut the onion in half through the root and peel it. Lay each half flat side down and dice it.
steps.tip: Hold the food with your hand shaped like a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

steps.text: Peel the garlic and slice each clove as thin as you can.
steps.tip: Lay the clove flat side down so it doesn't roll.

steps.text: Warm the olive oil in the skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring now and then, until soft.
steps.look: The onion is soft and see-through, just turning golden at the edges.

steps.text: Add the garlic, the oregano, and the chili flakes if you're using them. Stir for about a minute, until the garlic smells good and is just barely golden.
steps.tip: Garlic burns fast. Keep the spoon moving, and move on as soon as it smells good.

steps.text: Pour in the crushed tomatoes and add {qty:salt} salt. When it starts to bubble, turn the heat down to low so it simmers. Stir every few minutes until it thickens.
steps.tip: Pour the tomatoes slowly, close to the pan, so the hot oil doesn't splash.
steps.look: A spoon dragged across the pan leaves a path for a second.

steps.text: When the water is boiling hard, add the salt for the pasta water. Then add the spaghetti, and stir it with the tongs for the first two minutes so the strands don't stick together.
steps.tip: Lay the spaghetti in gently. Don't drop it from high up, or the water splashes.

steps.text: Boil the spaghetti, stirring now and then, until it's tender but still has a little bite in the middle.
steps.tip: Check the box for its time. Taste a strand when the timer rings, after letting it cool.

steps.text: Dip the liquid measuring cup into the pot and scoop out about 1 cup of the cloudy pasta water. Set it aside.
steps.tip: Wear an oven mitt on the hand holding the cup.

steps.text: Turn off the stove under the pasta. Set the colander in the sink. Carefully pour the spaghetti into the colander, tipping the pot away from you.
steps.tip: The steam rushes up when you pour. Keep your face back, and pour slowly.

steps.text: Tear the basil leaves into the sauce. Add the spaghetti to the sauce with the tongs and toss, adding splashes of the pasta water until the sauce coats every strand.
steps.look: The sauce clings to the spaghetti, glossy, with no puddle at the bottom of the pan.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Taste a strand, after letting it cool, and add a pinch more salt if it needs it. Serve with parmesan on top if you're using it.

move.title: Your sauce, your pasta
move.body: This is the unit's mastery cook. You'll cook frozen onion and jarred garlic in oil, simmer canned tomatoes into a sauce, boil the spaghetti, and drain it safely. You've done every step this unit. An adult is nearby; you run the kitchen.

wrong.fix: Start again with fresh oil and garlic. Burnt garlic makes the sauce bitter.
Simmer it a few more minutes with the lid off.
Toss it in the sauce with a splash of pasta water.

quiz.q: Why does the garlic go in after the onion?
How do you know the sauce has simmered enough?
choices: A spoon leaves a path across the pan

quiz.q: Which way do you tip the pot when you drain?
quiz.explain: The steam rises away from your face.

water-on.text: Fill the large pot with the water at the sink. Set it on the stove, cover it, and heat it on high.
water-on.tip: Carry it to the stove while it's still cold.

soften.text: Warm the oil in the skillet over medium heat. Add the frozen onion and stir now and then.

garlic-in.text: Stir in the garlic, oregano, and chili flakes for 1 minute.
garlic-in.tip: Keep the spoon moving. Garlic burns fast.

simmer.text: Pour in the tomatoes and the sauce's salt. When it bubbles, turn the heat to low.
simmer.look: A spoon leaves a path across the pan.
simmer.tip: Pour close to the pan so it doesn't splash.

salt-water.text: When the water boils hard, add the pasta's salt and the spaghetti. Stir with the tongs.

boil.text: Boil the spaghetti, stirring now and then.
boil.look: Tender, with a little bite in the middle.
boil.tip: Taste a strand after it cools.

save-water.text: With an oven mitt on, scoop 1 cup of pasta water into the measuring cup.

drain.text: Turn off that burner. Set the colander in the sink. Pour the pasta in, tipping the pot away from you.
drain.tip: Use oven mitts, and keep your face back.

toss.text: Tear the basil into the sauce. Add the spaghetti and toss with the tongs.
toss.look: Sauce on every strand, no puddle.
toss.tip: Add a splash of pasta water if it's dry.

serve.text: Turn off the stove. Taste a strand and add a pinch of salt if needed.
serve.tip: Top with parmesan if you like.
